prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates a near corridor and shelves from the darker rear rooms: across frames 1–3, most people are roughly 3–8 m ahead, while shelving and counters lie about 1–4 m away on both sides. The central person approaches from approximately 5–6 m in frame 3 to 2–3 m in frame 4 and about 0.5–1 m in frame 5, moving from near center to center-right and becoming close enough to be within the camera wearer's arm's reach only in the last frame; other people remain several metres behind and apart. It makes the approach, foreground-background ordering, and partial occlusion by shelves clearer than RGB, including the final person's upper body filling the view while the lower body and right side extend out of frame. Metric distances are only approximate, and the glowing shelves, clipped foreground surfaces, blurred boundaries, and inconsistent tones on walls and people make thin structures and exact separations unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates several people distributed from far left to right and distinguishes them from large fixtures, making overlap and visible extent easier to read than in RGB. In frames 1–2, small person masks correspond to people roughly 4–8 m away and separated by about 1–4 m laterally; a large fixture between them is incorrectly labelled "bus," while a central shelf or display in frame 3 is incorrectly labelled "refrigerator." The main person changes from a smaller central mask at roughly 4–5 m in frame 3 to a larger center-right mask around 2–3 m in frame 4 and a partly cropped mask around 0.5–1 m in frame 5, indicating approach and placing that person within arm's reach only at the end. The masks show foreground occlusion and out-of-view cropping, but they omit most shelves, walls, and some people, merge or fragment fine boundaries, provide no direct metric depth, and cannot reliably show gaze direction or whether one person is behind another without RGB/depth context.
descriptions.pose: The pose map provides joint geometry for the most detectable person in frames 2–5, clarifying body orientation and limb placement that motion blur obscures in RGB; frame 1 has no usable skeleton despite visible distant people. The frame-2 figure, roughly 4–6 m ahead, is upright and angled somewhat across the aisle, while the frame-3 figure at about 4–5 m is more front-facing or diagonally facing the camera wearer; exact gaze cannot be determined because facial orientation is not robustly represented. In frame 4 the larger torso skeleton, about 2–3 m away, is near center-right and broadly faces the camera, then in frame 5 the body becomes oversized and partly outside the right edge at about 0.5–1 m, with a magenta hand cluster near the lower torso that is within mutual arm's-reach distance. The changing skeleton scale supports approach and exposes partial-body occlusion, but missing legs, floating facial points, distorted limbs, duplicated or tangled hand joints, and absent poses for other people make exact reach, gaze, and inter-person spacing unreliable.
